0.0.n: A casual, masculine way to refer to yourself, used among close friends.

0.2.n: Names the activity that the speaker enjoys as a hobby.

0.3.n: Marks fishing as one example rather than an exhaustive list.

0.4.n: The speaker leaves out the particle marking fishing as the topic.

0.5.n: The plain form of です links fishing with being a hobby.

0.6.n: Follows だ to give the reason for the speaker’s choice.

0.8.n: Repeated here to contrast what the speaker personally would do.

0.9.n: This is the opening part of だったら, expressing a hypothetical situation.

0.10.n: Completes だったら; 俺だったら presents what the speaker would do in that situation.

0.11.n: The thing being taken; the object particle を is omitted in casual speech.

0.12.n: Presents a fishing rod as one possible item to bring.

0.13.n: 持つ in its て-form combines with いく to describe taking something to another place.

0.14.n: At the end of a suggestion, this softens the statement rather than introducing a clear contrast.

0.15.n: Adds a casual, reflective tone to the speaker’s personal choice.

1.0.n: Signals that the speaker has understood or accepted the previous idea.

1.2.n: A casual form of では that introduces a response based on what was just said.

1.3.n: お前 is a very familiar, potentially rude address; the attached 釣り combines with したら to mean doing some fishing.

1.4.n: The conditional form of する combines with いい to suggest an action.

1.5.n: いいじゃん casually endorses the suggestion; じゃん adds a sense of obviousness or encouragement.

1.7.n: This casual, masculine self-reference introduces the speaker’s own plan.

1.9.n: Names what the speaker will bring; casual speech leaves out を.

1.10.n: 持つ in its て-form plus いく describes taking an item to the destination.

1.11.n: Connects bringing a net with the offer that follows.

1.12.n: Points to whatever the other person catches or targets; the object particle を is omitted.

1.13.n: 釣る in its て-form plus あげる presents catching something as a favor to the listener.

1.15.n: Repeated after the offer to emphasize who will do the catching.

1.16.n: Marks 俺 as the person doing the action, with emphasis because it comes after the offer.

2.0.n: A rough, familiar address that fits this exasperated comeback.

2.1.n: The conditional form of いる imagines the listener being present.

2.2.n: Literally an island without people, which makes the other person’s presence the basis of the joke.

2.3.n: Together with the following ねえ, this forms the casual negative of だ.

2.4.n: A rough pronunciation of ない; 無人島じゃねえ denies that it is an uninhabited island.

2.5.n: Begins the ending じゃねえか, which forcefully points something out rather than reversing the earlier negative.

2.6.n: Another rough ない, this time inside the emphatic ending じゃねえか.

2.7.n: Makes the ending a rhetorical question, expressing protest rather than genuinely requesting an answer.

2.8.n: Adds force to the speaker’s annoyed realization.

0.lit: Me, fishing and such is a hobby, so if it were me, I’d take a fishing rod or something, though.
0.tip: 俺だったら means if it were me, a common way to introduce your own hypothetical choice.

1.lit: Oh, then you should fish. I’ll bring a net, so I’ll catch that for you, I will.
1.tip: A verb in its て-form plus あげる shows doing something as a favor for someone else.

2.lit: If you’re there, it’s not an uninhabited island, is it!
2.tip: The second じゃねえ belongs to the emphatic ending じゃねえか; it does not cancel the first negative.
